list.listitem: In caring for adults with intellectual disability (ID), assess their capacity for decision making using a tool adapted to the patient, consider their need for accommodations and supports, and identify with them a support person who can attend healthcare appointments and assist them as needed. B
Measurement of IQ and assessment of adaptive skills level are essential to diagnosis. C
Screening for inborn errors of metabolism, cytogenetic testing and neuroimaging should be ordered if not previously performed. B
Provide routine health maintenance consistent with national guidelines, noting increased risk of comorbid illness in cognitively-impaired adults. C
Conduct a periodic medication review with special attention to psychotropic medication use and polypharmacy and assess risk factors for abuse. C
Encourage education, sports, employment and community participation as ways to improve socialization and quality of life. B

background.definition: Mental retardation, now referred to as intellectual disability (ID) or cognitive impairment, is a cognitive disorder that is characterized by IQ less than 70, adaptive skills deficits, and onset before age 18 years.

list.listitem: Prevalence in the general population is approximately 1%.

Authors of a systematic review of 14 U.S. studies published since 2000 found a prevalence rate of IDs of 11.0 to 13.4 per 1000. In the only identified study of adults that incorporated Developmental Disability Act definitions, prevalence estimates for ID and/or developmental disability were 38.2 per 1,000 for children birth to 5 years, 31.7 for children 6 to 18 years, and 7.9 per 1,000 for adults.

Using a population database of children born from 1983 to 2010 in Western Australia, the overall prevalence of ID was 17.0/1000 livebirths (95% CI 16.7, 17.4) which was an increase from the 10-year previous prevalence of 14.3/1000. The prevalence of severe ID was 1.2/1000 livebirths.
People with an ID have a lower life expectancy, higher morbidity, and more difficulty obtaining healthcare than members of the general population.

In a systematic review, the most common chronic health conditions in children with ID were epilepsy (22.0/100), cerebral palsy (19.8/100), anxiety disorder (17.1/100), oppositional defiant disorder (12.4/100), Down syndrome (11.0/100), and autistic disorder (10.1/100); these prevalence rates are much higher than in the general population.

The pooled prevalence of a co-occurring psychiatric disorders in individuals with ID was 33.6% (95% CI 25.2%, 43.1%) based on a meta-analysis of 22 studies with high heterogeneity but no publication bias.

People with ID are at increased risk of diabetes compared to the general population with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.5 (95% CI 1.9-3.2). In this meta-analysis, the pooled prevalence of diabetes among 55,548 individuals with IDs was 8.5% (95% CI 7.2%-10.0%).

Adults with ID are also at higher risk of sexual assault (combined prevalence 32.9%; 95% CI 22.7-43.0; US prevalence 15.2%) and possibly partner violence victimization (60% identified in one non-representative sample).

Authors of a systematic review of 8 cohort and one quasi-experimental study of community-dwelling individuals with ID reported a rate of falls of 0.54 to 6.29 per person year and a rate of falls resulting in injury of 0.33 to 0.68 per person year. Based on 4 studies, the pooled proportion of people with ID who fell was 39%; 95% CI 35%, 43%. Evidence was rated as very low grade.
Most adults with IDs recognize that they are different and that others view them negatively; many express feelings of shame, anger and powerlessness.

Genetic abnormalities: 30%, most commonly Down syndrome and Fragile X syndrome. In one study, 11 mutations were found in 8 different synaptic genes encoding glutamate receptors among 95 people with nonsyndromic ID and none were found in healthy controls.
Congenital hypothyroidism, occurring in about 1 per 3000 births, causes intellectual disability in about 8% to 28% of children; in a 4 population study, the mean IQ was 85.
CNS malformation: 4%.
Fetal alcohol syndrome: 3%.
Thirty percent to 40% of causes are unknown.
The pathophysiology of mental retardation in most cases is unknown.

Mutations in the Ras-MAPK and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling cascades, originally identified as cancer regulatory pathways, appear to be critical for synaptic plasticity and behavior. Neurodevelopmental disorders arising from mutations in these pathways include ID, cognitive dysfunction, and autism.
See topics on Down syndrome, Fragile X, and Fetal Alcohol Syndrome for discussion of the pathophysiology of those conditions.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: African American, Hispanic, or Asian mothers

list.listitem: Screening for thyroid disease is indicated if there are signs and symptoms suggestive of thyroid disease. B

Vision and hearing screening: In one cohort study, pure-tone audiometry was successfully used for testing both ears in 90% of 1470 patients with mild to profound ID. Of those tested, about half failed the test and about half of those accepted referral for clinical evaluation. C
Lead screening in those with identifiable risk factors. B

In a review of 2 randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and 1 cohort study on preventive screening for community-dwelling individuals with ID, screening increased detection of vision and hearing problems and obesity, and increased women’s health screening and immunizations; most of the changes were intermediate steps toward improved health. B

Diagnosis should include IQ less than 70 on standardized assessment of intellectual functioning and adaptive functioning deficits in at least 2 areas with evidence of occurrence prior to age 18 years. C
Order metabolic screening for inborn errors of metabolism if not performed at birth, the results are not available, or if history or physical examination suggests a specific etiology. C
Cytogenetic testing should be performed. C
Neuroimaging is recommended as part of the work-up. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Nonverbal measures of IQ are normal and no impairment in adaptive functioning
Primary disturbance is in adaptive skills particularly communication and social skills
Primary impairment in short-term and working memory
Elevated blood lead level, possible cognitive deficits and clinical symptoms
Elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone, weight gain, dry skin, and depression

Diagnosis.Diagnostic_criteria: Must meet all 3 of the following criteria: IQ less than 70 when measured by standardized intellectual assessments. Adaptive skills deficits in at least 2 major categories: personal hygiene, communication, social skills, dressing, money management, shopping, meal preparation. Onset before age 18 years.

list.listitem: Take a thorough history including prenatal, perinatal, and neonatal course. Ask about previous newborn metabolic and lead screening.
Complete a careful developmental history including educational attainment and any previous cognitive evaluations.
Take a complete family history to ascertain presence of mental retardation in relatives.
Perform a thorough physical examination focusing on dysmorphic features of associated disorders such as Down Syndrome, Fragile X syndrome, or Fetal Alcohol Syndrome.
Request any previous neuroimaging studies.
Assess IQ using a standardized measure of intellectual functioning such as the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (4th ed) or Stanford Binet (5th ed).
Assess adaptive skills using a standardized tool such as the Vineland Adaptive Behavior Scales (2nd ed), Scales of Independent Behavior (revised) or Adaptive Behavior Assessment System (2nd ed).

Decision-making capacity can be assessed using tools such as the Informed voluntary consent checklist and sample questions found in Sullivan WF, ed. Developmental Disabilities Primary Care Initiative. Tools for the primary care for people with developmental disabilities. Available from: https://ddprimarycare.surreyplace.ca/tools-2/general-health/capacity-for-decision-making/.

Dementia in people with ID can be difficult to recognize. Authors of a systematic review found that the informant-based Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia in Down Syndrome Scale, the Cognitive Scale for Down Syndrome, and the Dementia Screening Questionnaire for Individuals with Intellectual Disabilities to be the best screening tools. For a more thorough assessment, they recommend the Cambridge Examination for Mental Disorders of Older People with Down's Syndrome and Others with Intellectual Disabilities.

Quality of life scales include for people with ID include the Quality of life in Late-Stage Dementia, shown to have good test characteristics, and the Dementia Quality of Life, with psychometric properties yet to be studied in individuals with ID.

Cytogenetic testing and neuroimaging are recommended as part of the work-up if not obtained previously or in childhood. Order metabolic screening if testing was not performed at birth, the results are not available, or if suggested by the history and physical examination.

Whole-exome sequencing, a technique for sequencing all expressed genes in a genome, can be used to detect potentially treatable inborn errors of metabolism among patients with intellectual developmental disorder and unexplained metabolic phenotypes. Using this process led to a diagnosis in 28 of 41 probands evaluated in one study.
EEG should be obtained if the history and physical examination suggest epilepsy.

If cognitive impairment is suspected, perform a thorough history and physical and a measure of intellectual functioning. Assess the patient’s capacity for decision making using a tool adapted to the patient, consider their need for accommodations and supports, and identify with them a support person who can attend healthcare appointments and assist them as needed.
Assess adaptive skills functioning (see Diagnostic Criteria) and confirm onset prior to age 18 years.
Targeted laboratory tests, cytogenetic testing and imaging are only recommended if indicated clinically or not performed during childhood.

Assess support needs. Among 7 measurement tools that may be useful for evaluating support needs of adults with ID, the two that have been used for individualized support planning and resource allocation are the supports intensity scale (SIS) and the instrument for classification and assessment of support needs (I-CAN), based on a systematic review.

Provide support and advocacy to patients and their families as access to healthcare and community services may be limited. A post-pandemic onset study using an online questionnaire of carers of children and adults with ID found 2 to 3 times greater reporting of a wish fulfilment coping style, defeat/entrapment, anxiety, and depression than reported in earlier pre-pandemic studies.

Heart rate monitoring (elevated >1 standard deviation above the daily mean and lasting >5 seconds) may be a useful marker of pain or distress in non-communicating persons with ID based on 1 small study.

The 2018 Canadian consensus guideline on primary care of adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities provides additional recommendations for approaches to care, health assessments, and management of physical and mental health needs.
Provide adaptive skills training, behavioral management, and psychiatric care for comorbid illness. C
Provide regular health maintenance visits to screen for comorbid illness, and provide preventive care, including evaluation of sexuality and fertility. C
Carefully screen for signs of abuse and neglect. C
Treat syndrome-specific physical disorders. C
Encourage exercise and sports participation, as able. C
There are no drug therapies for treating mental retardation. Drug therapy should focus on treating comorbid conditions.

Psychotropic medications are frequently prescribed for behavior problems in people with ID. In a systematic review and meta-analysis including 24 articles, pooled prevalence of use of psychotropic medications was 41% (95% CI 35-46%) including 31% on antipsychotics, 14% on antidepressants, 9% on anxiolytics, 5% on hypnotics/sedatives, and 1% on psychostimulants 1%. In another study, although some medication outcomes documented reduced repetitive, stereotypic, and/or aggressive behaviors, high dosing/prescribing in the setting of an absent/unclear clinical indication was associated with worsening of symptoms.

In one RCT of 25 patients taking risperidone for challenging behaviors, 9 of 11 randomized to discontinuation were successfully tapered completely off the medication over 14 weeks. At 8 weeks following medication discontinuation, there were no differences in irritability between those tapered off and those continued on medication and there were benefits of discontinuation on weight, waist circumference, prolactin levels and testosterone levels.

In one cross-over RCT of 23 adults with autism disorder and ID who had sleep difficulties, agomelatine, an atypical antidepressant, was effective and well tolerated for treating insomnia and circadian rhythm sleep problems.

Exercise interventions were assessed in a systematic review of RCTs and authors found inconsistent evidence of effectiveness in improving physical activity levels in individuals with ID. A multicomponent diet and physical activity program and a physical activity and fitness program improved physical activity levels.

In a second systematic review, exercise interventions to improve balance were effective in improving static and dynamic balance of young people with ID. Authors of another systematic review of 11 studies found moderate to strong evidence that physical activity interventions positively affected balance, muscle strength, and quality of life in individuals with ID. Twelve bi-weekly virtual gaming activity sessions were shown in a small RCT to improve balance in individuals with mild/moderate ID.
Exercise interventions also improved cardiovascular and muscular fitness of adults with mild/moderate ID.
Exercise alone does not appear to be sufficient to manage obesity in individuals with ID.
Water exercise may be useful for reducing muscular hypertonia in people with profound intellectual and multiple disability.

Interestingly, in an RCT including 30 adults with mild ID, training in Badminton for 12 weeks versus a control group receiving physical education improved domains of executive function for inhibitory control and working memory.

Sports participation can also confer benefits including improved function and reduced anxiety among those with ID. In a mixed methods study, benefits noted by participants with disabilities, some of whom had ID, included socialization opportunities, pure enjoyment, a sense of freedom, and providing an arena to challenge stereotypes.
Adaptive skills training may be of use to improve self-care skills, but published studies are lacking.
Social inclusion interventions were reported effective in creating better opportunities to engage in social interactions and improve social skills based on a systematic review of 24 studies.

Beginning reading interventions that include elements of phonologic awareness, letter sound instruction, and decoding, provided to children and adolescents with ID, are associated with small-to-moderate improvements in word reading, decoding, expressive and receptive language, and oral reading fluency.

Authors of a Cochrane review found low-quality evidence that parent training interventions improve some aspects of parenting such as safe home practice and parent-child interaction primarily for mothers with ID.

Authors of a systematic review found that secondary education increases employment among people with ID when it includes work experience and personal support services. Barriers to employment in the open market were the use of sheltered work, discrimination in vocational experience, class teaching, and deficient work experience. Facilitators of employment included support of one's family, employer and work organization; job coaching; a well-designed work environment, appreciation of one's work; and knowledge and experience of employment during secondary education.

Transitioning from employment to retirement can result in isolation. In an RCT including 29 Australian individuals with ID, 6 of 12 participants who received facilitation towards independent participation in mainstream community groups and volunteering were participating in an activity at 13 weeks compared to none of the 19 wait-list participants.

Use behavioral management if disruptive behavior is present. Authors of a meta-analysis of 22 studies found a moderate and long-lasting effect of non-pharmacological interventions (single and combinations of applied behavior analysis, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), mindfulness, relaxation, music, sensory stimulation and alternate response training) on challenging behaviors (d = 0.573, 95% CI 0.352-0.795). Interventions combining mindfulness and behavioral techniques appeared to be more effective than other interventions.

Authors of a systematic review of 17 studies concluded that there was a beneficial effect of multisensory therapy in some behavioral outcomes; however, there was no strong evidence that multisensory therapy was useful in reducing challenging behavior or stereotypic self-stimulating behavior.
Occupational training and participation may be effective in reducing challenging behavior.

Authors of a Cochrane review including 15 studies with 921 participants with ID found moderate-certainty evidence that cognitive-behavioral therapies such as anger management and positive behavior support can reduce outwardly-directed aggressive behavior in the short term; there is less certainty about effectiveness in the medium and long term, especially regarding quality of life outcomes.
Provide psychiatric care as needed for comorbid illness.
Regular health maintenance visits are recommended consistent with usual screening guidelines (noting special risk factors associated with certain conditions like Down syndrome).

Oral health is often poor among patients with IDs, including poor oral hygiene, gingivitis, periodontitis and untreated tooth decay, and should be preventable through regular toothbrushing and dental care. Authors of a Cochrane review, however, found unclear benefits of assessed interventions.
Dietary restriction for phenylketonuria and miglustat for Niemann-Pick disease type C can improve cognitive function for patients with those diseases.

Speech and language therapy may be helpful if evaluation supports the need. Authors of a systematic review of 10 studies, however, found insufficient evidence on effectiveness of these therapies on improving communication.

In a RCT of 12 adults with moderate ID and low speech intelligibility, both 6 weeks of conventional speech therapy and 6 weeks of Beatalk (imitating vocally-produced sounds and rhythms produced by a rhythm machine) improved articulation accuracy and voice measures, but larger gains were observed in the Beatalk group. In another study, use of smart speaker device for 12 weeks improved ratings of speech intelligibility in adults with intellectual disability compared to a control group for both smart speaker-related phrases and unrelated words.

Sexual and reproductive health needs should be addressed with patients and their caregivers. Authors of a scoping review highlighted the following areas to consider in these discussions: menstruation and menopause, vaccinations and preventive screenings, supporting sexuality and healthy relationships, coordinating with health-care providers, and contraception and sterilization.

In an RCT including 108 special education upper secondary school students with mild or moderate IDs, use of an educational invention including a Parenting Toolkit and Real Care Baby simulator increased knowledge and attitudes towards future parenting compared to the control group.

Conduct careful screening for signs of abuse and neglect. Authors of a systematic review found the following risk factors for abuse: female, more severe learning disability and communication difficulties, being known to services over time or since birth, having an escalation of challenging behavior, prior history of abuse, and involvement in an individual behavior management program or being in receipt of a drug to control behavior.

In residential settings, surveillance technology has been used to keep track of residents with dementia or intellectual impairment. In an ethnographic field study, investigators found that nurses in such facilities continue to do rounds, keep clients in close proximity, and lock doors at night. Identified problems with these systems included alarm fatigue leading to turning devices off and forgetting to take devices off when no longer needed.
Cochrane authors identified 7 trials of organizational interventions of healthcare services aimed at improving care of adults with ID, but none were clearly effective.
Shortened life expectancy when compared to the general population. B

In a population-based study in England of 247 people with intellectual disabilities who died, the median age at death for men was 65 years, 13 years younger than the median age at death of men in the general population, and the median age at death for women was 63 years, 20 years younger than the median age at death for women in the general population. Factors contributing to premature death included problems in advanced care planning, adherence to the Mental Capacity Act, living in inappropriate accommodation, adjusting care as needs changed, and caregivers not feeling heard.

The age-at-death discrepancy has decreased in recent years. In a study using data from 2005 to 2017 US death certificates, average age at death increased for those with ID from 60.3 years in 2005 to 63.4 years in 2017; a smaller increase was observed for those without intellectual or developmental disabilities (71.7 years to 72.5 years). Similar increases in average age at death were seen among adults with Down’s syndrome (54.1 years to 56.8 years) and cerebral palsy (50.3 years to 53.8 years).

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found higher rates of respiratory-associated deaths among adults with IDs (standardized mortality ratio [SMR] 6.53; 95% CI 4.29-9.96) compared with those in the general population and relatively high rates from pneumonia (SMR 26.65; 95% CI 5.63-126.24). Statistical heterogeneity of studies, however was high (I2 = 99.0%).
Cognitive level does not typically improve, but declines with age. B
Adaptive skills may improve with intervention but published studies are lacking. C

In addition to preventive care and management of chronic conditions, periodic screening and assessment of cognitive changes in adults with ID is important for identifying and helping to arrange services appropriate to their needs. Authors of a systematic review found the most widely used instrument for this assessment was the Dementia Questionnaire for Learning Disabilities. They discuss 39 scales, questionnaires, and inventories, and 13 batteries for assessing cognitive and behavioral changes in adults with ID in the paper.
Family homes and family caregivers are key supports for people with ID and should be encouraged to engage in future planning to ensure continued care and support with aging.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 23 studies with over 8 million women found that women with intellectual and developmental disabilities had an increased risk for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (pooled unadjusted OR 1.77, 95% CI 1.21, 2.60) and cesarean delivery (pooled unadjusted OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.02, 1.63).
